ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a ring of empty circles, with short lines connecting the circles in order, and the whole forms a closed loop. Counting them, there are 12 circles in total, and each circle is connected only to its two neighboring circles on the left and right, so after filling in 1 to 12, the adjacency relationship is a single closed 12-cycle containing 12 positions. Reasoning: Regard the numbers 1 to 12 as vertices of an auxiliary graph. Only when two numbers differ by 1 or 2 can they be adjacent in the original figure. The number 12 can differ by 1 or 2 only from 10 or 11, so in this closed loop, the two neighbors of 12 must be exactly 10 and 11. Next, 10 and 11 cannot be adjacent to each other again; otherwise 10-12-11-10 would form a smaller closed cycle, rather than a single closed loop using all 12 circles. Therefore the other neighbor of 11 cannot be 10, and can only be 9. Now look at 10: it is already adjacent to 12, and its other neighbor cannot be 11, so it can only be 8 or 9. If the other neighbor of 10 is 9, then 9-11-12-10-9 would form an independent 4-cycle, which is also impossible. Thus the other neighbor of 10 must be 8. So the pair of numbers that must be adjacent is 8 and 10.

raw_record.question_text: Joseph writes the numbers 1 to 12 in the circles so that the numbers in adjacent circles differ by either 1 or 2. Which pair of numbers does he write in adjacent circles?

method.method_draft: First read the diagram as 12 circles connected in one closed ring, so a valid filling is a single 12-cycle of the numbers. Treat numbers 1 through 12 as vertices of an auxiliary graph where two numbers may be adjacent only if their difference is 1 or 2. In this graph, 12 has only two possible neighbors: 10 and 11, so in the ring 12 must be adjacent to both 10 and 11. Then 10 and 11 cannot also be adjacent to each other, or 10-12-11-10 would form a smaller closed cycle inside the required single 12-cycle. Thus 11’s other neighbor must be 9. Now 10’s other neighbor, besides 12, can only be 8 or 9, since 10 cannot use 11. If it were 9, the four numbers 9-11-12-10-9 would form a separate 4-cycle, impossible in the one ring of 12 circles. Therefore 10’s other neighbor must be 8, so 8 and 10 are adjacent.
